back: Kernel data structure tracking PID, state, registers, and memory for a process.
analogy: Like a student ID and transcript.

back: The process of saving the state of the old process and loading the saved state for the new process.
analogy: Like pausing a video game and loading another save file.

back: A process that has terminated but still has an entry in the process table because its parent hasn't read its exit status.
analogy: Like a worker who quit but is still on the payroll until the boss signs off.

back: A process whose parent has terminated, usually adopted by the init process (PID 1).
analogy: Like a child whose parents left, so the state takes custody.

back: The smallest sequence of programmed instructions managed independently by a scheduler.
analogy: Like a single lane in a multi-lane highway.

front: What is User-level vs Kernel-level Threads?
back: User threads are managed by user libraries; kernel threads are managed directly by the OS.
analogy: Like hiring your own private security vs using the city police.

back: System call that creates a new process by duplicating the calling process.
analogy: Like cloning a sheep.

back: System call that replaces the current process image with a new program.
analogy: Like a brain transplant for a process.

back: System call used by a parent process to wait for a child process to finish.
analogy: Like a parent waiting outside school for their child.

back: Keeping multiple programs in main memory at the same time to maximize CPU utilization.
analogy: Like keeping multiple tabs open so you can switch instantly when one loads.

back: Logical extension of multiprogramming where CPU switches jobs so frequently that users can interact with each job.
analogy: Like a chef cooking 5 meals at once by taking turns.

back: Mechanisms like pipes, sockets, or shared memory allowing processes to communicate.
analogy: Like two different departments passing memos.

back: Optimization where parent and child share memory pages until one writes to it, at which point a copy is made.
analogy: Like sharing a read-only Google Doc until someone clicks 'Make a copy' to edit.

back: New, Ready, Running, Waiting/Blocked, Terminated.
analogy: Like the stages of a job application: Applied, Interviewing, Hired.

back: Module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler.
analogy: Like the usher who physically guides you to your seat.

back: Logical view of how a process is stored in memory, providing the illusion of a large, contiguous array.
analogy: Like having a massive virtual desk, even if your real desk is tiny.

back: Memory management scheme that eliminates the need for contiguous allocation of physical memory.
analogy: Like breaking a long book into pages that can be stored anywhere in a library.

back: Data structure used to map virtual pages to physical frames.
analogy: Like the library's index catalog mapping book chapters to shelf locations.

back: Hardware cache inside the MMU that stores recent virtual-to-physical address mappings.
analogy: Like a speed-dial list on your phone.

back: An interrupt that occurs when a program attempts to access a page that is mapped in address space, but not loaded in physical memory.
analogy: Like trying to read a book chapter that is in the basement, requiring you to fetch it first.

back: Bringing a page into memory only when it is needed.
analogy: Like ordering groceries only when you are about to cook the meal.

back: When the system spends more time paging (swapping pages) than executing instructions.
analogy: Like spending more time finding your tools than actually building the house.

back: Based on the assumption of locality, it defines the set of pages a process is currently using.
analogy: Like the tools you currently have out on your workbench.

back: Algorithm deciding which memory page to page out (e.g., LRU, FIFO, Clock).
analogy: Like deciding which old clothes to donate when your closet is full.

back: Replaces the page that has not been used for the longest period of time.
analogy: Like throwing away the spice you haven't cooked with in 3 years.

back: Phenomenon where increasing the number of page frames results in an increase in the number of page faults (happens in FIFO).
analogy: Like buying a bigger closet but somehow losing more clothes.

back: Memory management scheme that supports the user view of memory (logical segments like code, data, stack).
analogy: Like organizing a house by rooms (kitchen, bedroom) rather than equal-sized square blocks.

back: Moving entire processes between main memory and a backing store (disk).
analogy: Like packing up your entire desk and putting it in storage to make room for someone else.

back: Hardware device that maps virtual to physical address at run time.
analogy: Like an automatic GPS router.

back: A bit in the page table indicating if the page has been modified since it was loaded.
analogy: Like a 'needs to be saved' asterisk next to a filename.

front: What is CPU Burst vs I/O Burst?
back: Processes alternate between executing instructions (CPU burst) and waiting for I/O.
analogy: Like alternating between writing code and waiting for the compiler.

back: OS can interrupt a currently running process and move it to the Ready queue.
analogy: Like a boss pulling you off a task to handle an urgent fire.

back: Once a process gets the CPU, it keeps it until it terminates or switches to the waiting state.
analogy: Like a meeting you can't leave until it's finished.

back: The process that requests the CPU first is allocated the CPU first.
analogy: Like standing in line at a grocery store checkout.

back: Short processes get stuck waiting for one long CPU-bound process to finish in FCFS.
analogy: Like a line of sports cars stuck behind a slow tractor on a one-lane road.

back: Associates with each process the length of its next CPU burst, picking the shortest.
analogy: Like the express checkout lane for 10 items or fewer.

front: What is Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)?
back: Preemptive version of SJF.
analogy: Like letting someone with 1 item cut in front of you at the register.

back: Each process gets a small unit of CPU time (time quantum), then is preempted and added to the end of the queue.
analogy: Like passing a controller around so everyone gets a 5-minute turn playing a game.

back: The fixed time slice allocated to a process in Round Robin.
analogy: Like a 5-minute egg timer.

back: A priority is associated with each process, and the CPU is allocated to the highest priority.
analogy: Like VIP boarding at an airport.

back: A low priority process never gets to run because higher priority processes keep arriving.
analogy: Like never getting to ask a question because louder people keep interrupting.

back: Technique of gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait in the system for a long time (solves starvation).
analogy: Like gaining loyalty points the longer you wait in line.

back: Partitions the ready queue into several separate queues (e.g., foreground and background) with their own algorithms.
analogy: Like having separate lines for first-class, economy, and standby.

back: Allows a process to move between queues; separates processes according to the characteristics of their CPU bursts.
analogy: Like getting demoted to a slower lane if you take too long.

back: The interval from the time of submission of a process to the time of completion.
analogy: Like the total time from ordering pizza to eating it.

back: When multiple threads access shared data concurrently and the outcome depends on the order of execution.
analogy: Like two people trying to withdraw the last $100 from a joint bank account at the exact same time.

back: A segment of code where shared resources are accessed and must not be concurrently executed by more than one thread.
analogy: Like a single-occupancy public restroom.

back: If a process is executing in its critical section, no other processes can be executing in theirs.
analogy: Like only one person holding the talking stick.

back: A binary lock used to protect critical sections. The thread that acquires it must release it.
analogy: Like a physical key to the bathroom: you take it, use it, return it.

back: An integer variable used to control access to a common resource by multiple processes.
analogy: Like a bouncer holding a clicker, allowing exactly N people into a club.

back: A semaphore that can range over an unrestricted domain (used for managing N identical resources).
analogy: Like a parking garage counter showing available spots.

back: A semaphore whose value can only be 0 or 1, essentially acting like a Mutex.
analogy: Like a simple vacant/occupied sign.

back: Two or more processes are waiting indefinitely for an event that can be caused by only one of the waiting processes.
analogy: Like four cars at a 4-way stop each waiting for the car on their right to go first.

back: Mutual exclusion, Hold and wait, No preemption, Circular wait.
analogy: The four ingredients required to bake a deadlock disaster.

back: A deadlock avoidance algorithm that simulates resource allocation to ensure the system remains in a safe state.
analogy: Like a bank ensuring it has enough cash to satisfy its largest customer's maximum possible withdrawal.

back: Processes constantly change state in response to each other without making progress.
analogy: Like two people in a hallway constantly stepping to the same side to let the other pass.

back: A synchronization primitive that allows threads to wait until a particular condition occurs.
analogy: Like a pager from a restaurant that buzzes when your table is ready.

back: A high-level synchronization construct that encapsulates shared variables and the procedures that operate on them.
analogy: Like a class in object-oriented programming where all methods are automatically synchronized.

back: Classic sync problem where producers add data to a buffer and consumers remove it safely.
analogy: Like a chef putting burgers on a finite tray and a waiter taking them away.

back: Classic sync problem illustrating the challenges of allocating multiple resources to multiple processes.
analogy: Like needing two chopsticks to eat, but only having one between each person.

front: What is File Control Block / Inode?
back: Storage structure containing information about a file, including ownership, permissions, and location of file contents.
analogy: Like the metadata on a library catalog card.

back: The organization of files in a file system (flat, two-level, tree, acyclic-graph).
analogy: Like a system of folders and subfolders on your computer.

back: Each file occupies a set of contiguous blocks on the disk.
analogy: Like reserving an entire block of seats at a movie theater.

back: Each file is a linked list of disk blocks, which can be scattered anywhere.
analogy: Like a scavenger hunt where each clue tells you where the next clue is.

back: Brings all the pointers together into one location: the index block.
analogy: Like a table of contents that tells you exactly what page each chapter starts on.

back: An abstraction layer that allows the OS to support multiple file system types transparently.
analogy: Like a universal translator for different hard drive formats.

back: Keeps a log (journal) of changes not yet committed to the main file system to prevent corruption on crash.
analogy: Like taking notes on what you're going to write in ink before you actually write it.

back: A block of metadata that describes the characteristics of a file system (size, status, layout).
analogy: Like the blueprint and status report for the entire city infrastructure.

back: A directory entry that points directly to the inode of a file.
analogy: Like giving a person a second legal name; both names point to the exact same person.

back: A file whose data contains the path to another file.
analogy: Like a desktop shortcut or a sign pointing to another building.

back: The process of making a file system available to the OS at a specific directory (mount point).
analogy: Like plugging a new external hard drive into a specific USB port folder.

back: Redundant Array of Independent Disks; combines multiple drives into a single logical unit for performance or redundancy.
analogy: Like a team of horses pulling a carriage instead of just one.

back: Splits data evenly across two or more disks with no parity (high performance, no redundancy).
analogy: Like splitting a heavy load between two bags to run faster, but if one bag rips, you lose half your stuff.

back: Creates an exact copy of a set of data on two or more disks.
analogy: Like printing two copies of your essay just in case you lose one.

back: Block-level striping with distributed parity, requiring at least 3 disks. Tolerates 1 disk failure.
analogy: Like a magic trick where if one card is lost, you can perfectly guess it using the remaining cards.

back: Software that provides a high-level interface to a specific hardware device.
analogy: Like a translator who converts OS language into specific hardware language.

back: A signal emitted by hardware or software indicating an event that needs immediate attention.
analogy: Like a ringing doorbell interrupting your reading.

back: A software routine that hardware invokes in response to an interrupt.
analogy: Like the script you follow when you answer the doorbell (e.g., greeting the mailman).

back: An array of pointers to ISRs, indexed by interrupt number.
analogy: Like a phone directory telling you which department handles which type of emergency.

back: Allows hardware subsystems to access main system memory independently of the CPU.
analogy: Like hiring a mover to unload boxes directly into the living room without you having to carry each box.

back: Uses the same address space to address both memory and I/O devices.
analogy: Like assigning a specific room in your house to act as a mailbox.

back: The CPU repeatedly checks the status of a device to see if it is ready.
analogy: Like a kid in the back seat repeatedly asking 'Are we there yet?'

back: A device that moves data in structured blocks (e.g., hard drives, SSDs).
analogy: Like a shipping container that only moves large, fixed-size boxes.

back: A device that transmits data character by character (e.g., keyboards, mice).
analogy: Like a garden hose streaming water continuously.

back: Putting jobs in a buffer, a special area in memory or on a disk where a device can access them when it is ready.
analogy: Like a printer queue holding documents until the printer is free.

back: A memory area that stores data being transferred between two devices or a device and an application.
analogy: Like a waiting room at a doctor's office absorbing the mismatch in arrival times.

back: Storing a copy of data in a faster memory to speed up subsequent accesses.
analogy: Like keeping your most frequently used tools on your belt instead of in the shed.

back: Algorithms to determine the order in which disk I/O requests will be processed.
analogy: Like planning the most efficient route for a delivery truck.

back: The disk arm starts at one end, moves toward the other, servicing requests, then reverses direction.
analogy: Like an elevator picking up everyone on the way up, then everyone on the way down.

back: Like SCAN, but when it reaches the end, it returns to the beginning without servicing requests on the return trip.
analogy: Like a typewriter carriage returning quickly to start a new line.
